Figure 9.1 shows the standard incident response process advocated by CompTIA and covered on the CySA+ exam. This process was derived from revision two of NIST Special Publication 800-61. It is important to note that NIST released a new version of this document, NIST SP 800-61r3, in 2025, and that revision includes a new life cycle model. See the sidebar “The CSF-based Incident Response Life Cycle” for more on this model. We continue to use the model shown in Figure 9.1 in this book, as that is the model covered by the CS0-004 exam objectives.

Notice that this process is not a simple progression of steps from start to finish. Instead, it includes loops that allow responders to return to prior phases as needed during the response. These loops reflect the reality of responses to actual cybersecurity incidents. Only in the simplest of incidents would an organization detect an incident; analyze data; conduct containment, eradication, and recovery; perform post-incident activities; and close out the incident in a straightforward sequence of steps. Instead, the containment process often includes several loops back through the detection and analysis phase to identify whether the incident has been successfully resolved. These loops are a normal part of the cybersecurity incident response process and should be expected.

Preparation

CSIRTs do not spring up out of thin air. As much as managers may wish it were so, they cannot simply will a CSIRT into existence by creating a policy document and assigning staff members to the CSIRT. Instead, the CSIRT requires careful preparation to ensure that it has the proper policy foundation, has effective operating procedures tailored to the organization’s computing environment, receives appropriate training, and is prepared to respond to incidents.

The next two sections of this chapter, “Building the Foundation for Incident Response” and “Creating an Incident Response Team,” provide a more detailed description of the preparation phase.

The preparation phase also includes building strong cybersecurity defenses to minimize the likelihood and impact of future incidents. This process of building a layered approach to cybersecurity often includes many personnel who might not be part of the CSIRT.

During the preparation phase, the organization should also assemble the hardware, software, and information required to conduct an incident investigation. NIST provides lists of tools and resources that an organization’s incident response toolkit should include. Here are some of the essential items from those lists:

  • Digital forensic workstations
  • Backup devices
  • Laptops for data collection, analysis, and reporting
  • Spare server and networking equipment
  • Blank removable media
  • Portable printer
  • Forensic and packet capture software
  • Bootable USB media containing trusted copies of forensic tools
  • Office supplies and evidence collection materials

You’ll learn more about the tools used to conduct the incident response process in Chapter 10, “Evidence and Analysis,” and Chapter 11, “Containment, Eradication, and Recovery.”

The preparation phase of the incident response plan is not a “one and done” planning process. Notice in Figure 9.1 that there is a loop from the post-incident activity phase back to the preparation phase. Whenever the organization is not actively involved in an incident response effort, it should be planning for the next incident.

Detection and Analysis

The detection and analysis phase of incident response is one of the trickiest to commit to a routine process. Although cybersecurity analysts have many tools at their disposal that may assist in identifying an incident, many incidents are detected only because of the trained eye of an experienced analyst.

NIST describes four major types of indicators that may suggest an incident is underway:

  • Alerts that originate from intrusion detection and prevention systems, security information and event management systems, antimalware software, file integrity checking software, and/or third-party monitoring services.
  • Logs generated by operating systems, services, applications, network devices, and network flows.
  • Publicly available information about new vulnerabilities and exploits detected “in the wild” or in a controlled laboratory environment.
  • People from inside the organization or external sources who report suspicious activity that may indicate an incident is in progress.

When any of these information sources indicate that an incident may be occurring, cybersecurity analysts should shift into the initial validation mode, where they attempt to determine whether an incident is taking place that merits further activation of the incident response process. This analysis is often more art than science and is very difficult work. NIST recommends the following actions to improve the effectiveness of incident analysis:

  • Profile networks and systems to measure the characteristics of expected activity. This will improve the organization’s ability to identify abnormal activity during the detection and analysis process.
  • Understand the normal behavior of users, systems, networks, and applications. This behavior will vary between organizations, at different times of the day, week, and year, and in response to changes in the business cycle. A solid understanding of normal behavior is crucial for recognizing deviations from these patterns.
  • Create a log retention policy that specifies the information that must be logged by systems, applications, and network devices. The policy should also specify where those log records should be stored (preferably in a centralized log management system) and the retention period for logs.
  • Perform event correlation to combine information from multiple sources. This function is typically performed by a security information and event management (SIEM) system.
  • Synchronize clocks across servers, workstations, and network devices. This is done to facilitate the correlation of log entries from different systems. Organizations may easily achieve this objective by operating a Network Time Protocol (NTP) server.
  • Maintain an organization-wide knowledge base that contains critical information about systems and applications. This knowledge base should include information about system profiles, usage patterns, and other relevant details that may be useful to responders unfamiliar with the system’s inner workings.
  • Capture network traffic as soon as an incident is suspected. If the organization does not routinely capture network traffic, responders should immediately begin packet captures during the detection and analysis phase. This information may provide critical details about an attacker’s intentions and activity.
  • Filter information to reduce clutter. Incident investigations generate massive amounts of information, and it is basically impossible to interpret it all without both inclusion and exclusion filters. Incident response teams may want to create predefined filters during the preparation phase to facilitate future analysis efforts.
  • Seek assistance from external resources. Responders should be aware of the parameters for involving outside sources in their response efforts. This may be as simple as conducting a Google search for a strange error message, or it may involve full-fledged coordination with other response teams.

You’ll learn more about the process of detecting and analyzing an incident in Chapter 10.

The detection and analysis phase of incident response includes the initial identification and investigation of a cybersecurity incident. After this initial work, you remain in this phase as you prioritize the incident’s handling and notify key individuals.

Containment, Eradication, and Recovery

During the incident detection and analysis phase, the CSIRT engages in primarily passive activities designed to uncover and analyze information about the incident. After completing the initial detection and analysis, the team proceeds to the next phase, where they take active measures designed to contain the incident’s effects, eradicate it from the network, and restore normal operations.

At a high level, the containment, eradication, and recovery phase of the process is designed to achieve these objectives:

  1. Document the evidence.
  2. Select a containment strategy appropriate to the incident circumstances and implement the selected containment strategy to limit the damage caused by the incident.
  3. Eradicate the effects of the incident.
  4. Recover normal business operations.

You’ll learn more about the techniques used during the containment, eradication, and recovery phase of incident response in Chapter 11.

The containment, eradication, and recovery phase of incident response involves documenting evidence, isolating systems to contain the damage caused by an incident, eradicating the incident’s effects, and restoring normal business operations. The primary goal is to minimize the impact on the business.

Post-Incident Activity

Cybersecurity incidents don’t end after security professionals remove attackers from the network or complete the recovery effort to restore normal business operations. Once the immediate danger passes and normal operations resume, the CSIRT enters the post-incident activity phase of incident response. During this phase, team members conduct a root-cause analysis, write a report, and review lessons learned, ensuring that they meet evidence retention requirements.

Root-Cause Analysis

In the aftermath of an incident, cybersecurity analysts should develop a clear understanding of the incident’s root cause. This root-cause analysis is crucial to implementing a secure recovery that addresses any control deficiencies that contributed to the original attack. After all, if you don’t understand how an attacker breached your security controls in the first place, it will be hard to correct those controls so that the attack doesn’t succeed again!

Lessons Learned Review

During the lessons learned review, responders conduct a thorough examination of the incident and their response, with a focus on improving procedures and tools for future incidents. This review is most effective if conducted during a meeting where everyone is present for the discussion (physically or virtually). Although some organizations attempt to conduct lessons learned reviews in an offline manner, this approach does not facilitate the back-and-forth discussion that often yields the greatest insights.

The lessons learned review should be facilitated by an independent facilitator who was not involved in the incident response and is perceived by everyone involved as an objective outsider. This allows the facilitator to guide the discussion in a productive manner without participants feeling that the facilitator is advancing a hidden agenda. NIST recommends that lessons learned processes answer the following questions:

  • Exactly what happened and at what times?
  • How well did staff and management perform in dealing with the incident?
  • Were the documented procedures followed? Were they adequate?
  • What information was needed sooner?
  • Were any steps or actions taken that might have inhibited the recovery?
  • What would the staff and management do differently the next time a similar incident occurs?
  • How could information sharing with other organizations have been improved?
  • What corrective actions can prevent similar incidents in the future?
  • What precursors or indicators should be watched for in the future to detect similar incidents?
  • What additional tools or resources are needed to detect, analyze, and mitigate future incidents?

Once the group answers these questions, management must ensure that the organization takes follow-up actions, as appropriate. Lessons learned reviews are effective only if they surface needed changes and those changes then occur to improve future incident response efforts.

Evidence Retention

At the conclusion of an incident, the CSIRT has often gathered large quantities of evidence. The team leader should work with staff to identify both internal and external evidence retention requirements. If the incident may result in civil litigation or criminal prosecution, the team should consult with attorneys before discarding any evidence. If there is no likelihood that the evidence will be used in court, the team should follow any retention policies that the organization has in place.

At the conclusion of the post-incident activity phase, the CSIRT deactivates, and the incident-handling cycle returns to the preparation and detection and analysis phases.

U.S. federal government agencies must retain all incident-handling records for at least three years. This requirement appears in the National Archives General Records Schedule GRS 3.2, “Information Systems Security Records,” Item 20. See www.archives.gov/files/records-mgmt/grs/grs03-2.pdf for more information.

You’ll read more about the activities undertaken during the post-incident activity phase in Chapter 12, “Reporting and Communication.”

The CSF-Based Incident Response Life Cycle

When NIST published the incident handling life cycle that most practitioners are familiar with (and that CompTIA tests), security teams were still largely focused on on-premise systems, well-defined network perimeters, and a smaller number of high-value data repositories. Since then, incident response has expanded to include cloud services, SaaS dependencies, identity-centric attacks, supply chain compromises, and ransomware campaigns that blend technical disruption with business extortion. Modern response efforts must also account for faster regulatory reporting timelines, expanded third-party risk, and the reality that many incidents unfold across multiple environments and vendors at once.

Those changes influenced NIST’s 2025 update to the incident response guide, NIST SP 800-61r3. Rather than treating incident response as a stand-alone operational process, the new guidance frames incident response as part of an organization’s broader cybersecurity risk management program. This is where the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 becomes central: it provides a common language for describing security outcomes and linking day-to-day response work to governance, risk decisions, and business priorities.

CSF 2.0 is organized around high-level functions that describe what an organization is trying to achieve. In CSF 2.0, those functions are:

  • Govern
  • Identify
  • Protect
  • Detect
  • Respond
  • Recover

You can think of these as “verbs” that describe the outcomes an organization needs, from setting expectations and oversight (Govern) to restoring services and learning from disruptions (Recover). The strength of this approach lies in its alignment with incident response activities, utilizing the same structure as broader security planning and measurement.

Figure 9.2 shows the CSF-based incident response life cycle from NIST SP 800-61r3. The top portion of the figure highlights incident response activities within Detect, Respond, and Recover. The bottom portion shows preparation activities anchored in Govern, Identify, and Protect. Connecting the two is an Improvement component (shown as “(Identify) Improvement”) that captures lessons learned and drives updates back into both preparation and future incident handling.

This does not mean the older life cycle model was wrong. It remains a widely used, practical, and battle-tested way to organize the work of a CSIRT, and it is still the model you should study when preparing for the CS0-004 exam. The CSF-based approach is a modernization that enables organizations to integrate incident response into enterprise risk management, communicate more effectively with leadership, and measure whether their response capabilities are improving over time.

readings.title: Building the Foundation for Incident Response
readings.html:
One of the major responsibilities that organizations have during the preparation phase of incident response is building a solid policy foundation for the program. Every organization should have a set of policies, procedures, and playbooks that support the incident response program’s ongoing work. Organizations should also develop two key plans during this phase: an incident response plan that guides the team’s response activities and a communication plan that governs how the organization shares information during an incident.

Exam Tip

Incident response plans are closely related to an organization’s business continuity (BC) and disaster recovery (DR) programs.

The goal of the business continuity program is to ensure that the organization can maintain normal operations even during unexpected events. When an incident strikes, business continuity controls may protect the business’s core functions from disruption.

The goal of the disaster recovery program is to help the organization quickly recover normal operations if they are disrupted. An incident may cause service disruptions that would trigger the disaster recovery plan.

Due to the closely related nature of these programs, teams working on incident response should carefully coordinate their work with teams working on BC/DR efforts.

Policies

The incident response policy serves as the cornerstone of an organization’s incident response program. This policy should be written to guide efforts at a high level and provide the authority for incident response. The policy should be approved at the highest level possible within the organization, preferably by the chief executive officer. For this reason, policy authors should attempt to write the policy in a manner that makes it relatively timeless. This means the policy should contain statements that provide authority for incident response, assign responsibility to the CSIRT, and describe the role of individual users and state organizational priorities. The policy is not the place to describe specific technologies, response procedures, or evidence-gathering techniques. Those details may change frequently and should be covered in more easily changed procedure documents.

NIST recommends that incident response policies contain these key elements:

  • Statement of management commitment
  • Purpose and objectives of the policy
  • Scope of the policy (i.e., to whom it applies and under what circumstances)
  • Definition of events, cybersecurity incidents, investigations, and related terms
  • Roles, responsibilities, and authorities, such as which roles have the authority to confiscate, disconnect, or shut down technology assets
  • Guidelines for prioritizing incidents, estimating their severity, initiating recovery processes, maintaining or restoring operations, and other key actions
  • Performance measures

Including these elements in the policy provides a solid foundation for the CSIRT’s routine and crisis activities.

Procedures and Playbooks

Procedures provide the detailed, tactical information that CSIRT members need when responding to an incident. They represent the collective wisdom of team members and subject-matter experts collected during periods of calm and are ready to be applied in the event of an actual incident. CSIRT teams often develop playbooks that outline the specific procedures they will follow in the event of a particular type of cybersecurity incident. For example, a financial institution CSIRT might develop playbooks that cover:

  • Breach of personal financial information
  • Web server defacement
  • Phishing attack targeted at customers
  • Loss of mobile devices
  • General cybersecurity incidents not covered by another playbook

This is clearly not an exhaustive list, and each organization will develop playbooks that describe their response to both high-severity and frequently occurring incident categories. The idea behind the playbook is that the team should be able to pick it up and find an operational plan for responding to the incident that they may follow. Playbooks are especially important in the early hours of incident response to ensure that the team has a planned, measured response to the first reports of a potential incident.

For good examples of real-world cybersecurity incident playbooks, see the Ransomware Playbook (https://xsoar.pan.dev/docs/reference/playbooks/playbook3) or the Procedure for Windows Incident Response playbook from the University of Central Florida (https://infosec.ucf.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2019/07/Procedure_for_Windows_Incident_Response.pdf).

Exam Note

Playbooks are designed to be step-by-step recipe-style responses to cybersecurity incidents. They should guide the team’s response, but they are not a substitute for professional judgment. Responders handling an incident should possess the appropriate professional expertise and have the authority to deviate from the playbook when circumstances require a different approach.

Documenting the Incident Response Plan

When developing the incident response plan documentation, organizations should pay particular attention to creating tools that may be useful during an incident response. These tools should provide clear guidance to response teams that can be quickly read and interpreted during a crisis situation. For example, the incident handling checklist shown in Figure 9.3 provides a high-level overview of incident handling in checklist form. The CSIRT leader may use this checklist to ensure that the team doesn’t miss an important step in the heat of the crisis environment.

Documenting the Communication Plan

Responding to an incident is not solely a technical exercise. Throughout a response, the CSIRT must keep a variety of internal and external stakeholders informed about the incident, its impact, and the organization’s response efforts. Doing this well requires advance planning. Organizations should develop a communication plan that describes who must be notified during an incident, who is responsible for those communications, what information each audience should receive, and how quickly the communications must occur.

A communication plan reduces the risk of confusion and missteps in the high-pressure environment of an active incident. Without a plan, responders may inadvertently disclose sensitive details to the wrong audience, miss a regulatory reporting deadline, or send inconsistent messages that damage the organization’s credibility. The communication plan works hand in hand with the incident response policy, which establishes whether the CSIRT is authorized to communicate with external parties such as law enforcement and regulators.

Internal and External Audiences

The communication plan should identify each audience that may need information during an incident. Internal stakeholders typically include:

  • Senior leadership and the board of directors, who need timely, business-focused updates so they can make decisions about resources, risk tolerance, and public messaging
  • Legal counsel, who advise on regulatory obligations and may direct that certain communications occur under attorney-client privilege
  • Affected business units, which may need to adjust operations or implement workarounds
  • The broader employee population, who may need guidance on what they can and cannot share outside the organization

External stakeholders may include:

  • Customers whose data or services were affected by the incident
  • Regulators who require breach notification within specific timeframes
  • Law enforcement agencies that may investigate criminal activity
  • Business partners, vendors, and service providers connected to affected systems
  • Cyber insurance carriers, who often require prompt notification as a condition of coverage
  • Information sharing organizations, such as Information Sharing and Analysis Centers (ISACs), that help the broader community defend against similar attacks
  • The news media and the general public, particularly during incidents that attract attention

Designating Spokespeople

The communication plan should name the specific individuals authorized to speak on behalf of the organization. Centralizing external communication, often through a single spokesperson coordinated by the public relations team, helps ensure that messages are accurate and consistent. Individual responders and other employees should be instructed to refer outside inquiries to that spokesperson rather than commenting on their own.

Out-of-Band Communications

During an incident, the systems the CSIRT normally uses to communicate may themselves be compromised. An attacker with access to the corporate email system or chat platform could read the team’s messages and adjust the attack accordingly. For this reason, the communication plan should establish out-of-band communication channels that do not depend on potentially affected infrastructure. Options include personal phones, a separate messaging application, or a dedicated conference bridge. The team should identify and test these channels before they are needed.

Timing and Triggers

Many communications are time sensitive, and a growing number of laws and regulations require organizations to report breaches within tight windows. The European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), for example, requires notification of a supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of certain breaches. Other obligations arise from sector-specific regulations, securities laws, contracts, and state breach notification statutes, and these requirements change frequently. The communication plan should capture the obligations that apply to the organization and assign clear responsibility for meeting each deadline, with legal counsel tracking the current specifics.

Exam Note

Be sure you can distinguish the two plans developed during the preparation phase. The incident response plan guides what the team does during a response. The communication plan governs how and to whom the organization shares information about the incident. A strong communication plan addresses internal and external audiences, designates authorized spokespeople, includes out-of-band communication methods, and accounts for regulatory reporting deadlines.

readings.title: Creating an Incident Response Team
readings.html:
There are many different roles that should be represented on a CSIRT. Depending on the organization and its technical needs, some of these roles may be core team members who are always activated, whereas others may be called in as needed on an incident-by-incident basis. For example, a database administrator might be crucial when investigating the aftermath of a SQL injection attack but would likely be less helpful when responding to a stolen laptop.

The core incident response team typically consists of cybersecurity professionals with specialized expertise in incident response, known as incident handlers. In larger organizations, these may be full-time employees dedicated to incident response in a 24 × 7 security operations center (SOC). Smaller organizations may call on cybersecurity experts who fill other roles for their “day jobs” to step into CSIRT roles in the aftermath of an incident.

Organizations may also rely on external resources to support incident response. Managed security service providers (MSSPs) can provide monitoring, analysis, and response support, either as a supplement to an internal CSIRT or, in smaller organizations, as the primary incident response capability. Retaining an incident response MSSP gives the organization access to expertise that might not otherwise exist inside the firm. This may come at a significant expense, so organizations should decide what types of incidents can be handled internally and which require the use of an outside provider. Additionally, the organization should understand the provider’s guaranteed response time and ensure that it has a plan in place to respond to the early stages of an incident before the provider assumes control.

In addition, when incidents involve cloud platforms or other managed services, organizations may call upon the incident response teams of cloud service providers and key vendors, who often have greater visibility into their own infrastructure and specialized tools to support investigations. Due to this reliance on third parties, organizations should clearly define roles, responsibilities, and escalation paths in advance, enabling internal teams and external partners to respond quickly and effectively when an incident occurs.

The Role of Leadership

An organization’s leadership should play an active role in incident response efforts. The primary responsibility of senior IT and corporate leadership is to provide the authority, resources, and time required to respond appropriately to an incident. This includes ensuring that the CSIRT has the budget and staff required to plan for incidents and access to subject-matter experts during a response.

Leadership may also be called upon during an incident response to make critical business decisions about shutting down critical servers, communicating with law enforcement or the general public, and assessing the impact of an incident on key stakeholders.

In addition to the core team members, NIST suggests that the CSIRT include representation from the following:

  • Technical subject-matter experts whose knowledge may be required during a response. This includes system engineers, network administrators, database administrators, desktop experts, cloud experts, application experts, and privacy experts.
  • IT support staff who may be needed to carry out actions directed by the CSIRT.
  • Legal counsel who are responsible for ensuring that the team’s actions comply with legal, policy, and regulatory requirements and can advise team leaders on compliance issues and communication with regulatory bodies.
  • Human resources staff who are responsible for investigating potential employee malfeasance.
  • Public relations and marketing staff who can coordinate communications with the media and the general public.
  • Facilities staff who may be required to support physical security actions, such as securing buildings or controlling access to affected areas.
  • Asset owners who understand the business purpose and criticality of affected systems or data and can assist in prioritizing response actions and recovery efforts.

The CSIRT should be run by a designated leader with the clear authority to direct incident response efforts and serve as a liaison to leadership. This leader should be a skilled incident responder who is either assigned to lead the CSIRT as a full-time responsibility or serves in a cybersecurity leadership position.

CSIRT Scope of Control

The organization’s incident response policy should clearly outline the scope of the CSIRT. This includes answers to the following questions:

  • What triggers the activation of the CSIRT? Who is authorized to activate the CSIRT?
  • Does the CSIRT cover the entire organization, or is it responsible only for certain business units, information categories, or other divisions of responsibility?
  • Is the CSIRT authorized to communicate with law enforcement, regulatory bodies, or other external parties, and if so, which ones?
  • Does the CSIRT have internal communication and/or escalation responsibilities? If so, what triggers those requirements?

readings.title: Training and Testing
readings.html:
Building an incident response capability is not enough. The organization must also prepare its responders to execute that capability under pressure and verify that the plans actually work before a real incident puts them to the test. Training exercises serve both purposes at once. They walk team members through the processes they would follow during an incident and reveal gaps, ambiguities, and outdated assumptions in the plans, while there is still time to fix them.

The CySA+ exam focuses on two types of exercises: tabletop exercises and simulations. These sit on a spectrum from low-cost, discussion-based review to full hands-on rehearsal, and most organizations use a mix of both.

Tabletop Exercises

In a tabletop exercise, the response team gathers (physically or virtually) to discuss how they would respond to a hypothetical incident. A facilitator presents the scenario, often adding new developments as the discussion unfolds, and participants describe the actions they would take, the decisions they would make, and the resources they would call upon. No systems are touched and no production environment is affected.

Tabletop exercises are inexpensive and relatively easy to organize, which makes them a practical way to exercise the plan often. They are well suited to validating roles and responsibilities, surfacing gaps in procedures and playbooks, confirming that the communication plan reaches the right audiences, and familiarizing new team members with the process. Their main limitation is that they test what people say they would do rather than what they can actually do, so they may not surface technical problems or unrealistic time estimates.

Simulations

A simulation is a more sophisticated exercise that goes beyond discussion to actually exercise some or all of the organization’s incident response capabilities. Rather than describing their actions, responders carry them out, using the real tools, systems, and procedures they would rely on during an actual incident. A simulation might involve detonating sample malware in an isolated environment, walking through evidence acquisition on a staged host, or executing a containment procedure against a test system.

Simulations are more realistic than tabletop exercises and provide a much stronger test of whether the team and its tools perform as expected. They can validate technical skills, expose tooling problems, and produce realistic timing data. These benefits come at a cost. Simulations require more time, planning, and resources to conduct, and they carry some risk of disrupting operations if not carefully scoped and isolated from the production environment.

Exam Note

Know the difference between the two exercise types. A tabletop exercise is a discussion-based session in which the team works through a scenario without touching live systems. A simulation actually exercises the organization’s response capabilities using real tools and procedures. Tabletops are lower cost and easier to run frequently. Simulations are more realistic but require more time, resources, and care to avoid disrupting operations.

readings.title: Attack Frameworks
readings.html:
There have been many attempts to describe attack methodologies within frameworks, aiming to help defenders model attacks and develop appropriate defenses. The CySA+ exam focuses on three specific frameworks; however, your organization may use a different model or create its own, either from scratch or by combining one or more frameworks with its own requirements and experience. Attack frameworks are useful for helping you think through what an attacker is likely to do, so you can build appropriate defenses against attacks.

Mitre Att&ck

When cybersecurity analysts describe an attack, they often use the shorthand term TTPs, which stands for tactics, techniques, and procedures. Tactics describe the attacker’s objective, the “why” behind a set of actions. Techniques describe the general method used to achieve that objective, the “how” at a high level. Procedures describe the specific implementation details observed in the real world, such as the exact commands, tools, or scripts an attacker used in your environment.

MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) is a knowledge base that organizes these behaviors into a consistent structure that defenders can use to analyze incidents. The framework helps responders move from raw observations, such as logs, alerts, and forensic artifacts, to a clear description of what the adversary did and why it mattered. Because ATT&CK is a shared vocabulary, it also improves communication across teams and supports consistent reporting to leadership.

ATT&CK is organized into technology domains, representing the environments where adversaries operate. The three major domains are enterprise, mobile, and industrial control systems (ICS). Within each domain, ATT&CK identifies platforms, such as Windows or cloud environments, and then associates techniques and subtechniques with the platforms where they are applicable. This structure helps analysts focus their investigation and response efforts on the systems actually involved in an incident.

Figure 9.4 shows an example of the ATT&CK technique definition for active scanning techniques. It provides an ID number as well as classification details like the tactic, platforms it applies to, procedure examples, potential mitigating controls, and detection strategies.

In addition to the ATT&CK website and materials, a variety of third-party projects leverage ATT&CK to build playbooks, tools, and even commercial software. You can find the ATT&CK website at https://attack.mitre.org.

Diamond Model of Intrusion Analysis

When cybersecurity analysts investigate an incident, they are rarely just trying to answer the question “What happened?” They are also trying to understand who is behind the activity, how the attack was carried out, and what else they should be looking for in their environment. The Diamond Model of Intrusion Analysis provides a structured approach to considering these questions by describing intrusions as relationships between key elements, rather than as a simple sequence of steps.

In the Diamond Model, each observed malicious activity is treated as an event. Every event has four core features, represented as the vertices of the diamond:

  • The adversary, which represents the individual, group, or organization responsible for the malicious activity
  • The capability, which represents the tools, malware, exploits, or techniques the adversary used to carry out the attack
  • The infrastructure, which represents the systems, networks, domains, or services the adversary used to deliver, control, or support the attack
  • The victim, which represents the targeted organization, system, user, or data affected by the malicious activity

The model also includes meta-features that help analysts organize and connect events. These include items such as timestamp, phase, result, direction, methodology, and resources. Analysts use those details to link related events into activity threads, which show how a campaign unfolded over time, or to group events into clusters that share common characteristics. The Diamond Model also includes a confidence value that represents the analyst’s level of confidence in the support for the attribution and relationships provided by the available evidence.

Figure 9.5 shows an example of an analysis conducted for a compromised system. Note that each element helps to identify additional information or areas to review.

The Diamond Model places a strong emphasis on understanding the attacker and their motivations and then utilizes relationships between these elements to enable security analysts to both comprehend the threat and consider what additional data or information they may need to obtain or may already possess.

You can read the full text of the Diamond Model paper at https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/pdfs/ADA586960.pdf.

Cyber Kill Chain

The Cyber Kill Chain, developed by Lockheed Martin, is a seven-stage process, as shown in Figure 9.6.

The seven stages are as follows:

  1. Reconnaissance identifies targets. In this phase, adversaries plan their attacks and gather intelligence about the target, including both open source intelligence and direct acquisition of target data through scanning. Defenders must gather data about reconnaissance activities and prioritize defenses based on that information.
  2. Weaponization involves building or otherwise acquiring a weapon that combines malware and an exploit into a payload that can be delivered to the target. This may require creating decoy documents, selecting the appropriate command-and-control tool, and other specific details. The model emphasizes the need for defenders to conduct a thorough malware analysis at this stage, to understand not only what payload is dropped but also how the weaponized exploit was created.
  3. Delivery occurs when the adversary either deploys their tool directly against targets or via a release that relies on staff at the target interacting with it, such as in an email payload, on a USB stick, or via websites that they visit. Defenders in this stage must observe how the attack was delivered and what was targeted and then infer what the adversary intended to accomplish. Retention of logs is also important in this stage, as defenders need them to track what occurred.
  4. Exploitation uses a technical or human vulnerability to gain access. This can involve zero-day exploits and may use either adversary-triggered exploits or victim-triggered exploits. Defense against this stage focuses on user awareness, secure coding, vulnerability scanning, penetration testing, endpoint hardening, and similar activities to ensure that organizations maintain a strong security posture and a minimal attack surface.
  5. Installation focuses on persistent backdoor access for attackers. Defenders must monitor for typical artifacts of a persistent remote shell or other remote access methodologies.
  6. Command and Control (C2) access allows two-way communication and continued control of the remote system. Defenders will seek to detect the C2 infrastructure by hardening the network, deploying detection capabilities, and conducting ongoing research to ensure they are aware of new C2 models and technology.
  7. Actions on Objectives, the final stage, occurs when the mission’s goal is achieved. Adversaries will collect credentials, escalate privileges, pivot and move laterally through the environment, and gather and exfiltrate information. They may also cause damage to systems or data. Defenders must establish their incident response playbook, detect the actions of the attackers and capture data about them, respond to alerts, and assess the damage the attackers have caused.

The entire Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain can be found in greater detail at www.lockheedmartin.com/content/dam/lockheed-martin/rms/documents/cyber/Gaining_the_Advantage_Cyber_Kill_Chain.pdf.

Exam Note

The CySA+ exam objectives specifically call out three attack methodology frameworks: the Cyber Kill Chain, the Diamond Model of Intrusion Analysis, and the MITRE ATT&CK model. Be certain that you understand the details of these models before taking the exam!

chapters.title: Evidence and Analysis
chapters.essentials:
Understand evidence acquisition and preservation. Explain the basic concepts and process of evidence acquisition. Describe how evidence is commonly acquired and preserved as part of incident response activities, internal investigations, and due to legal holds as part of pending or current legal proceedings. Explain how data integrity validation is used to ensure that data matches the original source and has not been modified during either acquisition or analysis as part of the preservation process. Understand how and why chain of custody documentation is created and maintained for legal and police investigations but may also be created if investigations might become part of a legal proceeding. Explain why legal holds may require normal processes or procedures for data destruction or that limit lifespans of data to be suspended or why independent, verifiable copies may need to be made.

Describe triage and timelining in the context of incident analysis Explain the role of triage in incident response analysis. Describe the use of timelines as part of incident response processes including forensic analysis. Understand the major concepts related to analysis of incident response evidence analysis.

readings.title: Evidence
readings.html:
Evidence is used throughout the incident response process. Data about what has happened and the evidence of incidents and attacks is critical to investigations and responses. Without evidence, organizations are left with best guesses. That means knowing how to collect and analyze evidence is a critical skill for security practitioners.

One of the first steps to being able to perform evidence acquisition is having the right set of tools and capabilities to capture, collect, and analyze data that is useful as evidence. As part of this, organizations also need the ability to perform computer forensics for incident response purposes.

Exam Note

The CySA+ exam outline focuses on chain of custody, data integrity validation, preservation of evidence, and legal holds. There’s a lot more to the forensic and response process, but we will only cover it relatively lightly here to provide context as you prepare for the exam’s focus areas.

Evidence Gathering

Incident evidence often includes logs, files, drive images, and a variety of other artifacts that organizations may find useful in documenting and investigating an incident. That means organizations need to develop evidence gathering capabilities and processes before an incident occurs and to ensure that they know how they will acquire, document, and preserve data for both investigations and potential legal actions.

We will use the terms evidence gathering and evidence acquisition interchangeably. The CySA+ exam outline uses the term evidence gathering.

Forensic Procedures

One of the key ways that evidence is acquired is through forensic processes. Forensic analysis, sometimes called a forensic investigation, can take many forms, and there are a variety of formal models for forensic analysis, but the basic process involved when conducting them remains the same. In almost all scenarios you will take these steps:

  1. Determine what you are trying to find out. You may be asked to investigate a compromised system, to analyze the actions taken by malware, or to find out if a system administrator made an unauthorized change to a system. This forms the problem statement that helps to define what forensic activities you will take.
  2. Outline the locations and types of data that would help you answer the questions from step 1. Data may exist in many forms, and applications and systems can determine the format and accessibility of the data. Knowing where and how you need to collect data will also influence what your forensic process looks like. At this stage, you may not know the specific hardware or log locations, but you should be able to come up with the types of data and systems you will need to capture data from.
  3. Document and review your plan.
  4. Acquire and preserve evidence. The acquisition process may require drive imaging, cloning media, copying virtual machines or cloud instances, seizing systems or devices, or making live memory images to ensure that information is not lost when a system is powered off.
  5. Perform initial analysis, carefully tracking your actions, the systems and data you work with, and your findings, as well as any questions you need to answer.
  6. Use the initial analysis to guide further work, including deeper investigation, and review where the initial analysis pointed to additional data or where information is missing that is needed to answer the questions you originally asked.
  7. Report on the findings of the investigation.

Following a recognized forensic process can be helpful, particularly if you may be going to court. The NIST digital forensic process is a four-step methodology consisting of collection, examination, analysis, and reporting. This process systematically gathers evidence, processes it to identify relevant data, analyzes the findings to derive useful information, and documents the results in a formal report. You can review it as part of NIST SP 800-86, found at https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-86. While SP 800-86 is almost 20 years old, the basic concepts remain relevant today.

Drive Imaging

One of the most common parts of the evidence acquisition processes is drive imaging. Drive imaging creates a forensic copy of a drive using an imaging tool that makes a bit-stream (bit-by-bit) copy of the drive and then validates that the image matches the original drive. Most forensic image acquisition tools include hashing tools to perform this validation. A typical process includes:

  • Identifying what is needed to access the original drive. If the drive is removable, it may be removed and connected to a drive duplicator. If it is not removable, the system may be booted from forensic media, and the imaging software may then mount the drive for copying to a local or network connected device.
  • Imaging the drive, which can be time-consuming for large drives.
  • Validating a SHA256 or MD5 hash of the original drive and the image.
  • Documenting the forensic copy process and ensuring proper labeling for it.

Drive images are often prepared in native forensic formats like EnCase’s E01 format, or in a raw format like that provided by using the built-in Linux dd tool, which exactly preserves the binary dump of the drive.

Imaging Live Systems

When systems are using full-disk encryption or when applications, malware, or other software may be memory resident without a copy on the disk, an image may need to be collected while the system is running.

Live imaging may not obtain some desirable data:

  • Live imaging can leave remnants due to the imaging utility being mounted from a removable drive or installed.
  • The contents of a drive or memory may change during the imaging process.
  • Malware or other software may be able to detect the imaging tool and could take action to avoid it or disable it.
  • Live images typically do not include unallocated space.

Both commercial and open source tools provide portable versions that can be loaded on a live system to provide live imaging capabilities.

Acquiring Other Data

There are many other types of specialized data beyond drive images that you may want to specifically target during acquisition. Fortunately, in most cases, forensic images of the host drives will also provide access to that data if it is resident on the systems. A few of the other areas you may want to specifically target include log data, USB device histories, application data, browser cache and history, email, and user-generated files.

Acquiring and Reviewing Log Data

Log data is often stored remotely and may not be accurate in the case of a compromised machine or if an administrator was taking actions they wanted to conceal. At other times an investigation may involve actions that are logged centrally or on network devices, but not on a single local system or device that you are likely to create a forensic image of. In those cases, preserving logs is important and will require additional work.

To preserve and analyze logs:

  • Determine where the logs reside and what format they are stored in.
  • Determine the time period that you need to preserve. Remember that you may want to obtain logs from a longer period in case you find out that an issue or compromise started before you initially suspected.
  • Work with system or device administrators to obtain a copy of the logs and document how the logs were obtained. Checksums or other validation are often appropriate.
  • Identify items of interest. This might include actions, user IDs, event IDs, timeframes, or other elements identified in your scope.
  • Use log analysis tools like Splunk, Sawmill, Event Log Analyzer, or even a text editor to search and review the logs.

Acquiring Cloud Data

There are a wide variety of methods of acquiring cloud data depending on the type of cloud service and what data it creates, stores, and makes available. Many provide access via APIs or security tools like Amazon’s CloudWatch, CloudTrail, VPC flow logs, and S3 access logs. SaaS tools will often have audit logs available. Understanding the logs that are available, what configuration requirements, access methods, and limitations they may have as well as what costs may be associated with them are critical parts of cloud service adoption for most organizations.

There may be times where the log information you desire isn’t contained in the logs provided to you as a customer. Accessing the cloud provider’s own logs and systems is typically quite difficult and may require subpoenas or a court order.

Capturing Memory-Resident Data

Shutting down a system typically results in the loss of the data stored in memory. That means that forensic data like information in a browser memory cache or program states will be lost. Although capture information in memory isn’t always important in a forensic investigation, it is critical to be able to capture memory when needed.

There are a number of popular tools for memory captures, with a variety of capabilities, including the following:

  • fmem and LiME, both Linux kernel modules that allow access to physical memory. fmem is designed to be used with dd or similar tools; LiME directly copies data to a designated path and file.
  • DumpIt, a Windows memory capture tool that simply copies a system’s physical memory to the folder where the DumpIt program is. This allows easy capture to a USB thumb drive and makes it a useful part of a forensic capture kit.
  • The Volatility Framework supports a broad range of operating systems, including Windows, Linux, and macOS, and has a range of capabilities, including tools to extract encryption keys and passphrases, user activity analysis, and rootkit analysis.
  • Both EnCase and FTK have built-in memory capture and analysis capabilities as well.

Using Core Dumps and Hibernation Files

In addition to memory images, core dumps and crash dump files can provide useful forensic information, both for criminal and malware investigations. Since they contain the contents of live memory, they can include data that might not otherwise be accessible on the drive of a system, such as memory-resident encryption keys, malware that runs only in memory, and other items not typically stored to the disk.

The Windows crash dump file can be found by checking the setting found under Control Panel ➢ System And Security ➢ System ➢ Advanced System Settings ➢ Startup And Recovery ➢ Settings. Typically, full crash dump files will be located in the system root directory: %SystemRoot%\MEMORY.DMP. Windows memory dump files can be analyzed using WinDbg; however, you shouldn’t need to analyze a Windows kernel dump for the CySA+ exam.

Many of the techniques involved in a forensic investigation are useful for both incident response and internal investigations that may not have the same evidentiary requirements that a forensic investigation may require. This means it is often reasonable to bypass some of the strictest parts of chain of custody documentation and other procedural requirements—but only if you are absolutely certain that the investigation will not become a legal or police matter. When in doubt, it is safer to err on the side of over-documentation to avoid problems in court.

Acquisitions from Mobile Devices

Mobile device forensic acquisition typically starts with disabling the device’s network connectivity and then ensuring that access to the device is possible by disabling passcodes and screen lock functionality. Once this is done, physical acquisition of the SIM card, media cards, and device backups occurs. Finally, the device is imaged, although many devices may be resistant to imaging if the passcode is not known or the device is locked.

There are four primary modes of data acquisition from mobile devices:

  • Physical, by acquisition of the SIM card, memory cards, or backups
  • Logical, which usually requires a forensic tool to create an image of the logical storage volumes
  • Manual access, which involves reviewing the contents of the live, unlocked phone and taking pictures and notes about what is found
  • Filesystem, which can provide details of deleted files as well as existing files and directories

Once data has been acquired, mobile forensic tools can be used for the same types of analysis that are performed on PCs and servers.

Digital forensic tools for iOS and Android memory capture include commercial specialized mobile forensics suites like Cellebrite, Oxygen Forensic Detective, Magnet Axiom, and MOBILedit Forensic, which can extract data from mobile devices. The Autopsy open source forensic toolkit also supports analysis of data from both Android and iOS devices.

Triage and Evidence Acquisition

Organizations that are dealing with incidents often have to perform triage. This crucial first step in the forensic process drives selection of tools, targets, and how resources will apply to ensure that critical forensic data is not lost and that forensic targets receive attention in the right order. That also means practitioners need to determine if preserving information and evidence is more important than stopping an incident or returning to operational status. Making that call while deep in incident response processes can be difficult as you often won’t know what you’re losing or not preserving until after making a decision to move forward with restoration and response actions.

While it would be nice to always be able to choose to preserve all incident data while also stopping the incident and quickly returning to operations, organizations need to establish a decision process and guiding principles or a playbook around what they will try to preserve and how they will prioritize preservation and restoration activities.

The Police Are Here, Now What?

Organizational preferences for triage can be completely overridden when law enforcement gets involved. Once they’re part of your process, your decisions may be made for you, including whether your hardware or data remains in your control.

Engaging with law enforcement may be a choice, such as when an organization calls the police because they want their help or believe a crime has been committed, or it may be due to an investigation that brings the police to your door. If law enforcement shows up as part of an investigation, organizations will typically want to engage with their legal counsel to determine what they can and must do to respond. Knowing what level of cooperation and coordination is required—and desired—can have a major impact on how the process is handled.

Law enforcement engagement can also create unexpected issues. One of the authors of this book was involved in an incident investigation where local law enforcement was involved. A brand-new server that had been compromised was taken as evidence, leaving the department that was relying on it without their main server. They had to scramble as they had spent their budget and retired the old server but eventually worked around the missing device by putting the old server back into service. The bad news? The server didn’t get returned to the organization until almost six years later!

Determining Severity and Impact

The CySA+ exam outline points to the process of determining the severity and impact of an incident in addition to triage processes. NIST’s SP 800-61 provides some helpful guidance for organizations that want to use a common standard for impact, breaking impact into three categories. Functional impact and information impact are combined to determine the impact of the incident, while recovery effort helps to describe whether recovery can be completed with existing resources, if additional help will be needed, or if recovery is not possible.

  • Functional impact which focuses on the negative effect on the organization’s systems and operational capabilities.
  • Information impact is measured based on whether information as exfiltrated, and what type of information was exposed if any, as well as if information was deleted or changed.
  • Recoverability effort is determined by the time to recover and what types of resources may be required, as well as if recovery is possible.

You can review all of SP 800-61 at: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/61/r2/final.

Severity can be assessed by considering the criticality of the systems or services services, how broad the scope of the compromise is, the threat actor and their capabilities if known, and the data classification of data that was impacted. Severity levels vary by organization, but a 3-5 levels of severity classification are common.

Splunk provides a helpful breakdown of severity levels at: https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/learn/incident-severity-levels.html.

Severity and impact ratings help with incident prioritization, allowing organizations to spend effort where it will be most impactful and where the most significant problems are occurring.

Preserving Evidence

Regardless of the data types and acquisition methods, a key concept for evidence is preserving evidence, or preservation. Preserving data requires acquiring it, validating the acquisition and data, and storing it in a secure and documented manner. If the evidence may be required for a legal case or if law enforcement is involved, preservation will also typically require chain of custody documentation.

In addition to tactical and strategic choices about preservation, acquisition processes also need to take into account the order of volatility, which measures how easily data is to lose. This means data stored in memory or caches is considered highly volatile, since it will be lost if the system is turned off, whereas data stored in printed form or as a backup is considered much less volatile. Figure 10.1 shows a view of the order of volatility of common storage locations that data is likely to be acquired from during a forensic investigation.

Unexpected Forensic Discoveries

Forensic investigations can result in finding data that you did not intend to uncover as part of the investigation. Knowing what you will do if you find signs of issues or problems outside of the scope of the investigation you are conducting is helpful to avoid problems. This can be as simple as finding evidence of an employee violating company policies while investigating a compromise or as potentially complex as discovering evidence of illegal activities during an investigation. Make sure you know if you have a duty to report certain types of findings, under local, state, or federal law, or due to your own organization’s policies.

Preservation and Chain of Custody

In addition to simply preserving evidence, organizations may want or need to maintain chain of custody documentation. Chain of custody processes track evidence through its life cycle, including the collection, preservation, and analysis of the evidence. This requires documentation of who has access to the data, when, where, why, and how it is stored and used or transferred. Complete documentation of a chain of custody helps to ensure that the data was not inappropriately accessed or modified. Figure 10.2 (which may appear in the next section in some editions) shows an example of a chain of custody documentation form.

Creating and maintaining a chain of custody is particularly important for legal purposes including criminal investigations. If the chain is not properly created and maintained, questions about modifications or other actions may be raised in court, and evidence may not be allowed.

While maintaining a chain of custody doesn’t require multiple individuals, the “two-person rule” is a best practice to ensure integrity and prevent tampering. That means one person will perform the actions, and another will witness them, ensuring that both proper process if followed and that no tampering occurred.

Data Integrity Validation

Another important part of preservation activities is data integrity validation. To verify that the capture process did not inadvertently create changes, organizations work to ensure that the data captured and retained matches the original data. While this is critical for evidence and for legal cases, it is also important for organizational investigations to ensure that bad data doesn’t lead investigators to incorrect conclusions.

Data integrity validation is commonly accomplished using hashing tools that calculate a hash based on the original file, volume, or drive, and that then calculate a hash using the same algorithm against the copied evidence. These hashes are stored and validated when the copy is used to ensure that a matching copy is in use, as shown in FTK Imager in Figure 10.3.

Legal Hold

Legal holds (sometimes called litigation holds) are part of electronic discovery, or eDiscovery processes. Legal counsel will issue a legal hold notice to organizations when litigation is about to start or is underway. Data custodians in the impacted organization will be notified to preserve data, including data that might otherwise have been deleted or removed as part of normal business processes. This means that log rotation, automatic deletion of emails, or other processes that might delete data related to the litigation in process must be preserved and that the organization needs to figure out how to make that happen in an ongoing and consistent manner. Once a hold notice has been provided, the organization is obligated to preserve and produce the data as part of the legal process. Organizations may also undertake legal hold processes themselves if they expect to face lawsuits or other legal action.

If organizations don’t comply with legal holds or don’t implement them properly, a range of penalties can be imposed on them ranging from legal sanctions to judges instructing juries that they should assume the missing evidence would have been harmful to the organization that did not preserve it. That makes a solid, repeatable legal hold process critical for organizations.

You can read more about how legal holds are implemented in IaaS environments in Amazon’s documentation and review Microsoft’s documentation for Azure storage legal hold configuration options to help you think about what might be required for a legal hold’s technical aspects:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-backup/latest/devguide/legalhold.html
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cli/azure/storage/container/legal-hold?view=azure-cli-latest

readings.title: Evidence Analysis
readings.html:
Once you’ve collected and properly preserved evidence, you need to analyze it. That can include a variety of methods ranging from detailed forensic analysis to determine what happened during an incident or event to simpler techniques that are performed as part of incident response activities to quickly review evidence and form a thesis about what happened so that further response activities can occur.

Log Analysis

Organizations that gather log data as part of incident response and forensic activities need to analyze the log data and to identify additional log information that may be useful or relevant.

Most organizations will have a combination of local log files and centralized logs. While local log files will need to be gathered, centralized logs sent via syslog, Windows Event Forwarding, or some other means are critical to seeing and responding to events across entire organizations.

For many organizations that coordinated detection and response starts with their centralized security event and information management (SIEM) tool, or some other form of centralized log aggregation and analysis tool. There they will use rules and AI or machine learning capabilities to perform log correlation which matches logs and events together based on times, users, systems, or other data. SIEM tools and related technologies also provide alerts and notifications based on log information, leveraging correlation, rules, and thresholds to determine if an event or log should result in an alert ot notification being sent.

Incident responders often use command-line tools to analyze log data by using pattern matching and search tools like grep, awk, and sed as part of their response process.

Logs often benefit from log augmentation and enrichment which adds additional context to log data including IoC data, asset and user identity data, geolocation information, or vulnerability information.

Exam Note

The CySA+ exam outline points to log collection, log correlation, and log augmentation and enrichment. You should know about centralized and local logging, have an understanding of the role of SIEM devices and similar tools for log analysis and correlation, and be able to explain both what data would be useful for log augmentation and enrichment and how you might approach acquiring and using it.

Conducting a Forensic Analysis

Forensic analysis relies on more than just tools like a forensic toolkit or a forensic tools suite. The process of conducting a forensic investigation is often complex due to the number of systems, devices, individuals, and other material involved.

Forensic investigations conducted as part of an incident response process will often focus on root-cause analysis, the process of determining what happened and why. In addition, after the forensic investigation and incident response process is completed, lessons learned will be documented and acted on as part of the post-incident activity.

Tools of the Trade

There are a number of popular forensic tool options including commercial and open source solutions. These include:

Autopsy (https://www.autopsy.com/), an open source forensic toolkit

Opentext Forensic/EnCase (https://www.opentext.com/products/forensic), a commercial forensic tool

Exterro’s FTK Forensic Toolkit (https://www.exterro.com/digital-forensics-software/forensic-toolkit), a commercial forensic tool

The Volatility Framework (https://volatilityfoundation.org/the-volatility-framework/), an open source memory forensics tool

If you’ve never used a forensic toolkit before, it can help to work through exercises like those at the end of this chapter using a tool like Autopsy to better understand what is involved and what their capabilities are.

Evidence Handling

Drive and media images must be captured in a forensically sound manner that ensure that they match the original source. They require hashing as part of the process of validating data integrity, and with the exception of live system forensics where it cannot be completely avoided, forensic duplication should not change the source drive or device. To do this, an exact bit-for-bit copy is made using an imaging utility, write blockers are employed to prevent the possibility of modifying the source drive, and multiple copies are made so that the original drive can be retained for evidence.

You may discover that your investigation touches systems, networks, or data that you or your organization does not own. Company bring-your-own-device (BYOD) practices, cloud services, and employee use of third-party services for their private use on institutional systems can all complicate forensic examinations. Make sure you know your organization’s policies about each of those areas, as well as privacy policies and related standards, before you begin a forensic investigation.

Forensic Copies

Forensic copies of media don’t work the same way that simply copying the files from one drive to another would. Forensic copies retain the same layout and content for the entire device or drive, including the contents of “empty” space, unallocated space, and the slack space that remains when a file does not fill all the space in a cluster to ensure that deleted data or data that might exist due to drive re-mapping and other underlying maintenance activities can still be captured.

The need for a verifiable, forensically sound image means you need to use an imaging tool to create forensic images rather than using the copy command or dragging and dropping files in a file manager. Fortunately, there are a number of commonly available tools like dd or FTK’s Imager Lite built into major forensic suites that can create forensic images.

The Importance of Bit-by-Bit Copies

One reason that copies are not done using a copy command is to ensure that slack space and unallocated space are both copied as part of the image. This captures deleted files that have not yet been overwritten, fragments of older files in the space that was not written to by new files, and data that was stored on a drive before it was partitioned. Slack and unallocated space can provide rich detail about the history of a system, and simply copying files will not provide that visibility.

Handling Encrypted Drives

Drive and device encryption is increasingly common, making dealing with drive images more challenging. Of course, live system imaging will avoid many of the issues found with encrypted volumes, but it brings its own set of challenges. Fortunately, commercial forensic suites handle many of the common types of encryption that you are likely to encounter, as long as you have the password for the volume. They also provide distributed cracking methods that use multiple computers to attack encrypted files and volumes.

Using Write Blockers

Write blockers are an important tool for both forensic investigation and forensic drive image acquisition. During drive acquisition, using a write blocker can ensure that attaching the drive to a forensic copy device or workstation does not result in modifications being made to the drive, thus destroying the forensic integrity of the process. The same capability to prevent writes is useful during forensic analysis of drives and other media because it ensures that no modifications are made to the drive accidentally.

  • Hardware write blockers prevent writes from occurring while a drive is connected through them. Hardware write blockers can be certified to a NIST standard, and testing information is available via the NIST Computer Forensics Tool Testing program at www.cftt.nist.gov/hardware_write_block.htm.
  • Software write blockers are typically less popular than hardware write blockers, making them less common. Due to the possibility of problems, hardware write blockers are more frequently used when preventing writes from occurring is important.

Validating Data Integrity

Image verification is critical to ensuring that your data is forensically sound. Commercial tools use built-in data integrity verification capabilities to make sure the entire image matches the original. When investigators use dd or other manual imaging tools, md5sum or sha1sum hashing utilities are frequently used to validate images. Each time you generate an image, you should record the hash or verification information for both the original and the cloned copy, and that information should be recorded in your forensic logbook or chain of custody form. FTK’s Imager Lite will display the hash values in a report at the end of the process, as shown in Figure 10.4.

Reporting and Analysis

The final stage of forensic investigation is preparing and presenting a report. Reports should include three major components: the goals and scope of the investigation; the target or targets of the forensic activities, including all systems, devices, and media; and a complete listing of the findings and results.

Goals of the Investigation

This section of your report should include the goals of the investigation, including the initial scope statement for the forensic activities. This section will also typically include information about the person or organization that asked for the investigation. An example of a statement of the goals of an investigation is “John Smith, the Director of Human Resources, requested that we review Alice Potter’s workstation, email, and the systems she administers to ensure that the data that was recently leaked to a competitor was not sent from her email account or workstation.”

Targets

The report you create should include a list of all the devices, systems, and media that was captured and analyzed. All targets should be listed in your tracking notes and chain of custody forms if you are using them. The same level of detail used to record the system or device should be used in this listing. A sample entry might read:

Alice Potter’s workstation, internal inventory number 6108, Lenovo X1 Carbon, with Samsung SSD serial number S12KMFBD644850, item number 344

If large numbers of devices or systems were inspected, the full listing of targets is often moved to an appendix, and the listing of what was reviewed will list a high-level overview of systems, applications, devices, and other media, with a reference to the appendix for full detail.

Findings and Analysis

Findings are the most critical part of the document and should list what was discovered, how it was discovered, and why it is important. The Stroz Friedberg forensic investigation conducted as part of a contract dispute about the ownership of Facebook provides an example of the detail needed in forensic findings, as shown in Figure 10.5. While the report is now dated, many of the same forensic artifacts and concepts still show up—although floppy disks have been replaced with flash media and cloud storage!

Ars Technica has a copy of the full Stroz Friedberg forensic report from the public record for the case, and you can find it at https://cdn.arstechnica.net/wp-content/uploads/2014/08/strozreport.pdf.

Creating Timelines

Establishment of a timeline can be very helpful when using forensic techniques as part of incident response. Understanding what happened and when across filesystems, devices, and the entire event allows responders to determine if they identified all of the actions taken, understand what led to each step and what its result was, and consider how their own responses can be improved in the future.

Many forensics packages include timeline capabilities as part of their analysis suite, and organizations often build a timeline as part of their overall incident response report as well.

Lessons Learned

Once incident response has been completed, the final stage of post-incident activity is to identify lessons learned. These are the takeaways from the incident, including opportunities for improvement, new controls or practices that need to be implemented, and process or procedure changes that should be made.

Lessons learned can include a wide variety of feedback. They are used to drive the preparation phase of pre-incident work going forward.

Exam Note

The CySA+ exam outline uses broad terms here: analysis, triage, and establishing a timeline. As you prepare for the exam, make sure you have a solid grasp on how you’d analyze evidence from an incident, how you would prioritize actions as part of a triage process, and how you would use a timeline as part of both incident response and post incident reporting.

chapters.title: Containment, Eradication, and Recovery
chapters.essentials:
Explain the purpose of containment activities. After identifying a potential incident in progress, responders should take immediate action to contain its scope and impact. They should select appropriate containment strategies based on the nature of the incident and its impact on the organization. Potential containment activities include network segmentation and removal of affected systems.

Know the importance of collecting evidence during a response. Much of the evidence of a cybersecurity incident is volatile in nature and may not be available later if not collected during the response.
