NIST describes root-cause analysis as “A principle-based, systems approach for the identification of underlying causes associated with a particular set of risks” in both SP 800-30 and SP 800-39, but neither standard actually describes how to accomplish one! The good news is that INST does provide RCA guidance: https://www.nist.gov/system/files/documents/2016/11/22/guidelines_for_the_use_of_root_cause_analysis_to_reduce_error_and_improve_quality_in_forensic_science_labs.hollway.labmgmt.pdf.

Lessons Learned

Knowing how and why an incident occurred doesn’t help organizations if they don’t apply the knowledge. That means that conducting a lessons-learned exercise or analysis is critical to preventing similar issues and incidents from occurring in the future. Lessons-learned processes focus on figuring out how to prevent future issues rather than on blame, and they should be used to drive changes and the implementation of appropriate controls.

Shift and Incident Handover: Staffing Incidents

A final consideration in both reporting and communication is ensuring that shift and incident handover processes allow for processes to continue without interruption. As you consider security operations and incident response, be sure to think about what handovers need to provide continuity. That often includes:

  • A status update or briefing process
  • Documentation about what was accomplished
  • Lists of open tasks, findings, and similar information
  • Plans for staff change-overs

While each organization will handle this differently, it is critical to build processes for staffing continuity in advance of an issue or event.

Managing shift hand-offs and incident handovers isn’t just important from a reporting and communication basis. In fact, it should be baked into your incident response process and playbooks, as teams become less effective as incidents drag on. It’s always good to know in advance who will take over and how you’ll manage incidents that run over multiple shifts, multiple days, or even multiple weeks or months!

Exam Note

As you prepare for the exam, make sure you pay attention to after-action reporting concepts including conducting lessons-learned activities and root-cause analysis. Consider how you’d address shift and incident handover and how you’d build internal threat intelligence reports tailored to the organization and threats it faces based on incident data.

Incident Response Metrics and KPIs

The CySA+ exam objectives point to eight measures that you should consider as you think about incident response. These are likely to be found not only in incident response reports but are also commonly part of ongoing reporting for security organizations:

  • Alert volume is less frequently used because it is difficult to ascribe meaning to a given volume. It may mean organizations have not properly tuned their alerts, it may mean that the organization has few effective alerts, or it could also mean that the organization has an effective detection system and has tuned their alerts and that only critical alerts are raised. Thus, relying on alert volume as a metric or KPI is often seen as a flawed measure. A more useful measure would be whether alerts occurred for incidents and resulted in the IR process activating or if incidents were discovered in other ways, meaning that alerts were not properly configured to discover them.
  • False-positive rate based KPIs consider how often the organization incorrectly identifies something that isn’t actually true. A common example in vulnerability management is false positives for vulnerabilities. If an organization has a high false-positive rate for vulnerabilities, it will spend unnecessary time and effort attempting to remediate vulnerabilities that do not exist.
  • True-positive rate is the mirror of the false-positive rate. True-positive rates assess how often assessments are correct. Organizations will seek a high true-positive rate with a low false-positive rate to ensure that they are correctly identifying vulnerabilities.
  • Mean time to close describes the average time it takes to close a vulnerability remediation process or other task. If an organization has a KPI established with a goal of seven days as the mean time to close a newly discovered vulnerability, on average, vulnerabilities should be corrected within seven days of being found.
  • Mean time to detect is how long it took from the initial event that resulted in an incident to when it was detected. This requires forensic analysis to determine accurately but can be a meaningful measure for organizations that are seeking to determine if their detection capabilities are suited to the threats they face. Organizations facing advanced persistent threats have found that they’ve been compromised for months or years at a time without detection, which would result in a very poor statistic for mean time to detect!
  • Mean time to respond measures the time from detection to assessing the event as an incident and activating the process. It’s important to differentiate that from the next metric, mean time to remediate, as remediation can vary based on the size and complexity of the incident.
  • Mean time to remediate is a much more complex measure to provide a metric for since each incident’s size, scope, and complexity will all influence the mean time to remediate. This metric requires more nuanced communication and explanation than a simple number on a report in many cases and may benefit from granular reporting describing types of incidents as well as their impact and scope.
  • Phishing campaign click rates are tracked as part of organizational preparedness and awareness assessments and are often required by cybersecurity insurance providers.

Organizations seeking to implement metrics and KPIs need to understand both what they are measuring and why they are measuring it. Simply providing numbers without meaningful context or a process to use the metrics and KPIs will not serve to improve incident response processes and reporting and may actually consume resources that are needed elsewhere.

prompt.html:
An organization suffered a successful ransomware attack that encrypts several critical file servers. After containing the attack, the IT team wipes the affected systems, reinstalls the operating systems, and restores all data from clean backups so that normal operations can resume.

What control function is primarily being performed when the team restores from backup and rebuilds the servers?

questions.explanation: Restoring from backup and rebuilding wiped servers is a classic example of a corrective control, because it focuses on returning systems and data to a known good state after an incident has already occurred. Preventative controls are designed to stop ransomware from succeeding in the first place, such as patching, access controls, or application allow listing. Detective controls are aimed at identifying or alerting on malicious activity, like IDS alerts, log monitoring, or file integrity checks. Responsive controls involve immediate reaction or containment to limit damage, such as isolating affected hosts from the network or disabling compromised accounts. In this scenario, those containment actions have already happened, and the activity described is specifically about repair and restoration of normal operations, which is the role of corrective controls.

Detective controls are aimed at identifying or alerting on malicious activity, like IDS alerts, log monitoring, or file integrity checks. prompt.text: STRIDE is an example of what?

questions.explanation: STRIDE is a threat modeling methodology because it is a structured framework used to categorize and analyze potential threats to a system based on spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, and elevation of privilege. It is not a zero-day rating system, as it does not assign scores or ratings to previously unknown vulnerabilities. It is not a vulnerability assessment tool, since it does not scan systems or directly detect vulnerabilities but rather guides thinking about possible threats. It is also not an adversary analysis tool, because it focuses on types of threats and their impact on system components rather than profiling specific attackers or their capabilities.

Wiping the server is an eradication step that would destroy evidence and is unjustified without confirmation of compromise. Reviewing media reports does not provide environment-specific context and cannot reliably distinguish legitimate migration traffic from malicious activity on that particular server.

questions.explanation: Mimikatz is a tool the attacker uses to carry out an action, so it represents the Capability vertex because it reflects the technical means, software, and techniques used to achieve the intrusion objectives. The adversary vertex is the person or group operating the tool rather than the tool itself; infrastructure refers to the systems and services the attacker uses to communicate or stage activity such as domains, IPs, or servers rather than the credential dumper; and victim refers to the targeted organization and affected workstation rather than the attacker’s tooling.

prompt.text: Alice is responding to a cybersecurity incident and notices a system that she suspects is compromised. She places this system on a quarantine VLAN with limited access to other networked systems. What containment strategy is Alice pursuing?
prompt.html: Alice is responding to a cybersecurity incident and notices a system that she suspects is compromised. She places this system on a quarantine VLAN with limited access to other networked systems. What containment strategy is Alice pursuing?

questions.explanation: Putting the suspected compromised system onto a quarantine VLAN with limited ability to communicate with other networked systems is isolation, because the goal is to contain the incident by segmenting the affected host and preventing lateral movement or further damage while preserving it for investigation. Eradication focuses on eliminating the threat from the environment by removing malware, closing vulnerabilities, and ensuring the attacker no longer has a foothold. A honeypot is a deliberately deployed decoy system meant to attract and study attackers rather than a method for restricting a real, potentially infected production host. Removal generally refers to removing malicious components or affected assets from service or deleting them, which goes beyond simply restricting network connectivity.

prompt.text: An analyst seizes multiple thumb drives as part of an incident investigation. The drives contain evidence that may be used in court. Which action is MOST important to ensure the evidence remains admissible?
prompt.html: An analyst seizes multiple thumb drives as part of an incident investigation. The drives contain evidence that may be used in court. Which action is MOST important to ensure the evidence remains admissible?

options.label: A
options.text: Use purging or clearing to remove sensitive data from the drives
options.html: Use purging or clearing to remove sensitive data from the drives

options.label: C
options.text: Reimage drives and return them to their owners
options.html: Reimage drives and return them to their owners

options.label: D
options.text: Physically destroy the drives as they were involved in an incident and can no longer be trusted
options.html: Physically destroy the drives as they were involved in an incident and can no longer be trusted

questions.explanation: Maintaining a detailed evidence log is most important because it establishes and preserves chain of custody, showing who handled the thumb drives, when and where they were stored, and what actions were taken with them, which is essential for evidence to be accepted in court. Purging or clearing would alter or destroy the data, invalidating the evidence rather than preserving it. Reimaging the drives would overwrite original contents and eliminate the very artifacts that need to be presented. Physically destroying the drives prevents any further analysis and guarantees the evidence cannot be produced in legal proceedings.

questions.explanation: When Alice encounters a false positive error in her scans, her first action should be to verify it. prompt.text: A security architect is concerned that developers are unknowingly pulling vulnerable third-party and open source libraries into a new microservices-based application. The architect wants an automated process that scans source repositories and container images to discover all third-party components and compares them against vulnerability databases on an ongoing basis. Which security approach best meets this requirement?
prompt.html:
A security architect is concerned that developers are unknowingly pulling vulnerable third-party and open source libraries into a new microservices-based application. The architect wants an automated process that scans source repositories and container images to discover all third-party components and compares them against vulnerability databases on an ongoing basis.

Which security approach best meets this requirement?

questions.explanation: Software composition analysis best fits this scenario because it is specifically designed to inventory third-party and open source components in code bases and container images and continuously compare them against known vulnerability databases, which directly addresses the concern about vulnerable libraries being pulled into a microservices application. Static application security testing focuses on analyzing proprietary source code for security flaws such as injection or logic errors, not on identifying and tracking third-party components. Dynamic application security testing evaluates running applications from the outside by sending requests and analyzing responses, which can reveal runtime issues but does not provide a comprehensive bill of materials for libraries and their known CVEs. Manual code review depends on human reviewers and is time-consuming and error-prone for identifying all third-party components across many microservices, and it lacks the continuous, automated vulnerability correlation that the architect is seeking. To learn more on this topic, see Chapter 8 .
questions.explanationHtml: Software composition analysis best fits this scenario because it is specifically designed to inventory third-party and open source components in code bases and container images and continuously compare them against known vulnerability databases, which directly addresses the concern about vulnerable libraries being pulled into a microservices application. Static application security testing focuses on analyzing proprietary source code for security flaws such as injection or logic errors, not on identifying and tracking third-party components. Dynamic application security testing evaluates running applications from the outside by sending requests and analyzing responses, which can reveal runtime issues but does not provide a comprehensive bill of materials for libraries and their known CVEs. Manual code review depends on human reviewers and is time-consuming and error-prone for identifying all third-party components across many microservices, and it lacks the continuous, automated vulnerability correlation that the architect is seeking. To learn more on this topic, see Chapter 8.
